Stochastic homogenization of the Keller-Segel chemotaxis system

Anastasios Matzavinos  and Mariya Ptashnyk Affiliation:  Division of Applied Mathematics, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912, USA Affiliation:  Division of Mathematics, University of Dundee, Dundee, DD1 4HN, UK Affiliation:  Computational Science and Engineering Laboratory, ETH Zürich, CH-8092, Zürich, Switzerland
Abstract

In this paper, we focus on the Keller-Segel chemotaxis system in a random heterogeneous domain. We assume that the corresponding diffusion and chemotaxis coefficients are given by stationary ergodic random fields and apply stochastic two-scale convergence methods to derive the homogenized macroscopic equations. In establishing our results, we also derive a priori estimates for the Keller-Segel system that rely only on the boundedness of the coefficients; in particular, no differentiability assumption on the diffusion and chemotaxis coefficients for the chemotactic species is required. Finally, we prove the convergence of a periodization procedure for approximating the homogenized macroscopic coefficients.

Keywords: Chemotaxis, stochastic homogenization, two-scale convergence, Palm measures, point processes.

1 Introduction

Chemotaxis as a term refers to the directed movement of cells and microorganisms in response to a chemical signal. Historically, the first mathematical model of chemotaxis was proposed by Keller and Segel in order to investigate the aggregation dynamics of cellular slime molds, such as the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum [30]. Since then, the Keller-Segel model has been analyzed extensively, and a comprehensive review of related mathematical results can be found in the two articles by Horstmann [23, 24].

It is well known that in one dimension the Keller-Segel model is well-posed globally in time. Global existence and boundedness of solutions in one dimension were first shown by Yagi [46] by means of energy estimates. Moreover, the well-posedness and the existence of a finite-dimensional attractor for the one-dimensional model was proved by Osaki and Yagi [41].

The dynamics of the Keller-Segel model in two and three dimensions are more complex than the one-dimensional case, since in higher dimensions the solutions may blow up in finite time [27, 38, 45, 47]. Several results that appeared in the 1990’s have demonstrated that in two and three dimensions the Keller-Segel model is well-posed globally in time for “small” initial data. However, in the presence of “large” initial data, the solutions blow up; in other words, they do not remain bounded [25, 26, 39, 46].

Corrias and Perthame [11] showed that in dd dimensions, the Keller-Segel model is critical in Ld/2L^{d/2}, which is to say that the “smallness” or “largeness” of the initial data is determined in terms of the Ld/2L^{d/2} norm. Similar conditions were derived in [12, 13] for a parabolic-elliptic variation of the Keller-Segel model. The global behavior of a two-dimensional parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system, under the assumption of “small” initial data, was investigated by Gajewski and Zacharias [18].

As alluded to in the above paragraphs, there is a wealth of results on the existence and regularity of solutions of the Keller-Segel model. However, there is no literature investigating homogenization approaches and the influence of substrate heterogeneity on the dynamics of the model.

Stochastic homogenization is a growing field in multiscale analysis. Some of the first results on the stochastic homogenization of linear second-order elliptic equations were obtained by Kozlov [32] (by a direct contraction of the corrector functions), by Papanicolaou and Varadhan [43] (by using Tartar’s energy method), and by Zhikov et al. [50] (by using GG-convergence of operators). Subsequently, the homogenization of quasi-linear elliptic and parabolic equations with stochastic coefficients was considered by Bensoussan and Blankenship [6] and Castell [10]. The stochastic homogenization of convex integral operators by means of Γ\Gamma-convergence was considered by Dal Maso and Modica [15, 16]. The method of viscosity solutions was employed by Caffarelli et al. [9] to derive effective equations for fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations in stationary ergodic media. In a similar fashion, subadditive ergodic theory has been used together with the theory of viscosity solutions or variational representations of solutions and the minimax theorem to homogenize Hamilton-Jacobi and viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations in stationary ergodic media [2, 31, 34, 35] (see also references therein). More recently, subadditive ergodic theory has also been employed to homogenize quasiconvex (level-set convex) and, more generally, non-convex Hamilton-Jacobi equations in stationary ergodic media [3, 4].

The theory of periodic two-scale convergence [1, 37, 40] has been extended in the stochastic setting by Bourgeat, Mikelić, and Wright [8], who defined the concept of two-scale convergence in the mean, and by Zhikov and Piatnitski [52], who defined an explicitly stochastic two-scale convergence for random measures. The two-scale convergence in the mean has been applied to derive macroscopic equations for single- and two-phase fluid flows in randomly fissured media [7, 49]. The stochastic two-scale convergence has been extended to Riemannian manifolds and has been applied to analyze heat transfer through composite and polycrystalline materials with nonlinear conductivities [20, 21].

The paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we formulate a microscopic chemotaxis model with diffusion and chemotaxis coefficients for the chemotactic species given by stationary ergodic random fields. In contrast, and consistent with the experimental setting discussed in section 2, the diffusion coefficient of the chemical species (chemoattractant) is assumed to be deterministic, i.e., independent of the random medium. We then derive a priori estimates in section 3 and prove the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions for the microscopic model. Our derivation of the a priori estimates differs from those found in [22], [39], or [41], as we only assume the boundedness of the rapidly oscillating coefficients describing the stochastic medium. In section 4, we use the derived a priori estimates and the notion of stochastic two-scale convergence to derive a macroscopic (homogenized) model for our system. Two auxiliary stochastic problems are obtained to define the macroscopic diffusion and chemosensitivity coefficients for the chemotactic species. In section 5, we use a periodization procedure and prove the convergence of the effective coefficients obtained by periodic approximation to the corresponding macroscopic coefficients obtained by the stochastic homogenization approach of section 4.

2 Formulation of the problem

We consider a variation of the original Keller-Segel model of chemotaxis [30], where the coefficients of the model are defined by stationary random fields. Specifically, we consider the system:

utε\displaystyle u^{\varepsilon}_{t} =\displaystyle= ∇⋅(Duε(x)∇uε−χε(x)uε∇vε),x∈Q,t>0,\displaystyle\nabla\cdot(D_{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)\nabla u^{\varepsilon}-\chi^{\varepsilon}(x)u^{\varepsilon}\nabla v^{\varepsilon}),\;\;\quad x\in Q,\,t>0, (1)
vtε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon}_{t} =\displaystyle= ∇⋅(Dv(x)∇vε)−γvε+αuε,x∈Q,t>0,\displaystyle\nabla\cdot(D_{v}(x)\nabla v^{\varepsilon})-\gamma v^{\varepsilon}+\alpha u^{\varepsilon},\;\;\quad x\in Q,\,t>0,
∂uε∂n=0,∂vε∂n=0,x∈∂Q,t>0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial u^{\varepsilon}}{\partial n}=0,\quad\frac{\partial v^{\varepsilon}}{\partial n}=0,\quad x\in\partial Q,\,t>0,
uε(0,x)=u0(x),vε(0,x)=v0(x),x∈Q,\displaystyle u^{\varepsilon}(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\;\quad v^{\varepsilon}(0,x)=v_{0}(x),\;\quad x\in Q,

where Q⊂ℝdQ\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is a bounded domain and α\alpha, γ\gamma are positive constants. Moreover, uεu^{\varepsilon} and vεv^{\varepsilon} denote the density of a population of cells (the chemotactic species) and the concentration of a chemoattractant, respectively.

As will become apparent in the following, the parameter ε{\varepsilon} represents the spatial scale of the microscopic structure of the underlying medium or substrate. The diffusion coefficient DuεD_{u}^{\varepsilon} and the chemosensitivity function χε\chi^{\varepsilon} depend on ε{\varepsilon}, as they are affected by changes in the properties of the substrate. It is assumed that these changes do not affect the diffusion of chemicals, and specifically the diffusion coefficient DvD_{v} does not depend on ε{\varepsilon} (nonetheless, we allow for DvD_{v} to be a smooth enough function of the spatial variable xx). This is consistent with in vitro experiments where the cells are positioned on a micropatterned surface, and hence their random and chemotactic motility are affected by the microstructure, whereas the chemoattractant diffuses freely in the solution above the surface [19].

In order to specify the dependence of the model coefficients on the microscopic scale ε{\varepsilon}, we introduce the concept of a spatial dynamical system as follows (see, e.g., [8]). We consider a probability space (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P) with probability measure PP. Throughout the paper, Ω\Omega is assumed to be a compact metric space and ℱ\mathcal{F} is the σ\sigma-algebra of Borel sets over Ω\Omega. We define a spatial dynamical system 𝒯⁡(x):Ω→Ω{\mathcal{T}}(x):\Omega\to\Omega, i.e. a family {𝒯⁡(x):x∈ℝd}\{{\mathcal{T}}(x)\,:\,x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\} of invertible maps, such that for each x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, both 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) and 𝒯−1​(x){\mathcal{T}}^{-1}(x) are measurable and satisfy the following conditions:

  1. (i)

    𝒯⁡(0){\mathcal{T}}(0) is the identity map on Ω\Omega and 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) satisfies the semigroup property:

    𝒯⁡(x1+x2)=𝒯⁡(x1)​𝒯​(x2) for all ​x1,x2∈ℝd.{\mathcal{T}}(x_{1}+x_{2})={\mathcal{T}}(x_{1}){\mathcal{T}}(x_{2})\quad\text{ for all }x_{1},\,x_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
  2. (ii)

    PP is an invariant measure for 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x), i.e. for each x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} we have that

    P⁡(𝒯−1​(x)​F)=P⁡(F).P({\mathcal{T}}^{-1}(x)F)=P(F).
  3. (iii)

    For each F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}, the set {(x,ω)∈ℝd×Ω:𝒯⁡(x)​ω∈F}\{(x,\omega)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\Omega:{\mathcal{T}}(x)\omega\in F\} is a d​x×d​P​(ω)dx\times dP(\omega)-measurable subset of ℝd×Ω\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\Omega, where d​xdx denotes the Lebesgue measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

The coefficients in (1) are defined as follows. First, we define two stationary random fields through the relations

Du​(x,ω)=D~u​(𝒯⁡(x)​ω)​ and ​χ​(x,ω)=χ~​(𝒯⁡(x)​ω),D_{u}(x,\omega)=\widetilde{D}_{u}({\mathcal{T}}(x)\omega)\,\mbox{ and }\,\chi(x,\omega)=\widetilde{\chi}({\mathcal{T}}(x)\omega),

where D~u\widetilde{D}_{u} and χ~\widetilde{\chi} are given measurable functions over Ω\Omega. Then, given the specified assumptions on the random fields, the coefficients Duε​(x)D_{u}^{\varepsilon}(x) and χε​(x)\chi^{\varepsilon}(x) are defined as

Duε​(x)=Du​(x/ε,ω)​ and ​χε​(x)=χ⁡(x/ε,ω).D_{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)=D_{u}(x/{\varepsilon},\omega)\,\mbox{ and }\,\chi^{\varepsilon}(x)=\chi(x/{\varepsilon},\omega).

From a mathematical point of view, this construction of the coefficients is common in the stochastic homogenization literature because it allows for the use of ergodic theory in the asymptotic investigation of (1) as ε→0{\varepsilon}\rightarrow 0 (see section 4). From a modeling perspective, this construction is equivalent to the assumption that the coefficients are statistically homogeneous (see, e.g., [14]). As alluded to above, the chemoattractant diffusion coefficient DvD_{v} does not depend on ε{\varepsilon}.

As an example, we discuss here a specific construction of (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P) and 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) based on the Poisson point process in order to provide some intuition on the abstract setting discussed above. Consider the case where motile cells are positioned on a micropatterned surface with randomly imprinted “dots,” i.e. Duε​(x)D_{u}^{\varepsilon}(x) and χε​(x)\chi^{\varepsilon}(x) are assumed to attain distinct values in the union of randomly dispersed balls and in their exterior. Then, a realization ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega is identified with a set ω={B⁡(𝜶m):m∈ℕ}\omega=\{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{m})\,:\,m\in\mathbb{N}\} of a spatial distribution of balls B⁡(𝜶m)B(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{m}) of a specified radius centered at 𝜶m\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{m}, and the σ\sigma-algebra ℱ\mathcal{F} is defined as follows. Let N⁡(ω,A)N(\omega,A) denote the number of balls the centers of which fall in the open set A⊂ℝ2A\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}. Then, ℱ\mathcal{F} is the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the subsets of Ω\Omega of the form

{ω∈Ω:N(ω,A1)=k1,…,N(ω,Ai)=ki},\{\omega\in\Omega\,:\,N(\omega,A_{1})=k_{1},\ldots,N(\omega,A_{i})=k_{i}\},

where i,k1,…,kii,k_{1},\ldots,k_{i} are non-negative integers and A1,…,AiA_{1},\ldots,A_{i} are disjoint open sets. A natural choice for the probability measure PP (in the absence of any a priori information) is given by the Poisson point process defined in the following way. We let

P⁡(N⁡(ω,A1)=k1,…,N⁡(ω,Ai)=ki)=P⁡(N⁡(ω,A1)=k1)×…×P⁡(N⁡(ω,Ai)=ki),P\bigl(N(\omega,A_{1})=k_{1},\ldots,N(\omega,A_{i})=k_{i}\bigr)\,=\,P\bigl(N(\omega,A_{1})=k_{1}\bigr)\times\ldots\times P\bigl(N(\omega,A_{i})=k_{i}\bigr),

with

P⁡(N⁡(ω,A)=k)=(λ​|A|)kk!​exp⁡(−λ​|A|),P\bigl(N(\omega,A)=k\bigr)\,=\,\frac{(\lambda|A|)^{k}}{k!}\exp(-\lambda|A|),

where λ\lambda is a positive parameter. In this setting, 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) is defined as the family of translation operators given by:

𝒯⁡(x)​ω={B⁡(𝜶m)+x:m∈ℕ},{\mathcal{T}}(x)\,\omega=\{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{m})+x\,:\,m\in\mathbb{N}\},

where x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and ω={B⁡(𝜶m):m∈ℕ}\omega=\{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{m})\,:\,m\in\mathbb{N}\}. One can define a metric that turns Ω\Omega into a compact metric space, as required in the more general setting of section 2. This can be achieved either by considering an alternative characterization of the Poisson point process as a point process over i.i.d. compact domains that cover the Euclidean space (see, e.g., [14]) or by using an appropriate weighting and normalization of one of the standard sequence space norms (see, e.g., [29]). This specific construction of (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P) and 𝒯⁡(x)\mathcal{T}(x) is intuitive from a modeling perspective. Nonetheless, the somewhat more abstract setting of a spatial dynamical system is quite versatile, and will be adopted in the remainder of the paper.

3 Existence of solutions of the microscopic problem and a priori estimates

In this section, we establish a priori estimates for the weak solutions of (1) that eventually lead to the proof of our main homogenization result in section 4. In what follows, we distinguish (and treat differently) the cases dim​(Q)=1\text{dim}(Q)=1 and dim​(Q)≥2\text{dim}(Q)\geq 2. In the latter case, motivated by experimental and modeling settings for biological and physical systems, we only consider the cases dim​(Q)=2\text{dim}(Q)=2 and dim​(Q)=3\text{dim}(Q)=3. However similar results can also be obtained when dim​(Q)≥4\text{dim}(Q)\geq 4.

If dim​(Q)=1\text{dim}(Q)=1, the chemotaxis system has a global solution as shown in [22, 41, 46]. However, since the system studied in this paper has fast oscillating diffusion and chemotaxis coefficients, we provide a different proof of the well-posedness of the system than the one developed in [22, 41, 46]. Specifically, our derivation of the a priori estimates does not require the differentiability of DuεD^{\varepsilon}_{u} or χε\chi^{\varepsilon}.

Theorem 3.

Under Assumption 1 and dim​(Q)=1\text{dim}(Q)=1 there exists a unique weak solution of (1) for every ε>0{\varepsilon}>0, and for PP-a.s. ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega we have

‖uε‖L∞​(0,τ,L2​(Q))+‖∂xuε‖L∞​(0,τ,L2​(Q))+‖∂tuε‖L2​(Qτ)≤C,‖vε‖L∞​(0,τ,H1​(Q))+‖∂tvε‖L2​(0,τ,H1​(Q))+‖∂x2vε‖L∞​(0,τ,L2​(Q))≤C,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\|u^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q))}+\|\partial_{x}u^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q))}+\|\partial_{t}u^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(Q_{\tau})}\;\leq C,\\ &\|v^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}(0,\tau;H^{1}(Q))}+\|\partial_{t}v^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(0,\tau;H^{1}(Q))}+\|\partial^{2}_{x}v^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q))}\;\leq C,\end{aligned} (5)

for any τ>0\tau>0, where the constant CC is independent of ε{\varepsilon}.

Proof.

The existence of a weak solution to problem (1) is proved by showing the existence of a fix point of the operator KK defined on L4​(0,τ,W1,4​(Q))L^{4}(0,\tau;W^{1,4}(Q)) by vε=K⁡(v¯ε)v^{{\varepsilon}}=K(\overline{v}^{{\varepsilon}}) with vεv^{{\varepsilon}} given as a solution of the linear problem

utε=\displaystyle u^{{\varepsilon}}_{t}= ∂x⋅(Duε(x)∂xuε−χε(x)uε∂xv¯ε)\displaystyle\partial_{x}\cdot(D_{u}^{{\varepsilon}}(x)\,\partial_{x}u^{{\varepsilon}}-\chi^{\varepsilon}(x)\,u^{{\varepsilon}}\,\partial_{x}\overline{v}^{{\varepsilon}})\;  in ​Qτ,\displaystyle\text{ in }Q_{\tau}\;, (6)
vtε=\displaystyle v^{{\varepsilon}}_{t}= ∂x⋅(Dv(x)∂xvε)−γvε+αuε\displaystyle\partial_{x}\cdot(D_{v}(x)\,\partial_{x}v^{{\varepsilon}})-\gamma\,v^{{\varepsilon}}+\alpha\,u^{{\varepsilon}}\;  in ​Qτ,\displaystyle\text{ in }Q_{\tau}\;,
∂xuε=0,∂xvε=0\displaystyle\partial_{x}u^{{\varepsilon}}=0,\qquad\;\qquad\partial_{x}v^{{\varepsilon}}=0  on ​(0,τ)×∂Q,\displaystyle\text{ on }(0,\tau)\times\partial Q\ \;,
uε​(0,x)=u0​(x),vε​(0,x)=v0​(x)\displaystyle u^{{\varepsilon}}(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\;\quad v^{{\varepsilon}}(0,x)=v_{0}(x)\;  in ​Q.\displaystyle\text{ in }Q\;.

By applying Galerkin’s method [17] and a priori estimates similar to the estimates (10), (15), (17), and (18) established below, we obtain for every v¯ε∈L4​(0,τ,W1,4​(Q))\overline{v}^{{\varepsilon}}\in L^{4}(0,\tau;W^{1,4}(Q)) the existence of solutions (uε,vε)(u^{{\varepsilon}},v^{{\varepsilon}}) of (6) with uε∈L2​(0,τ,H1​(Q))∩H1​(0,τ,L2​(Q))u^{{\varepsilon}}\in L^{2}(0,\tau;H^{1}(Q))\cap H^{1}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q)) and vε∈H1​(0,τ,L2​(Q))∩L∞​(0,τ,H2​(Q))v^{{\varepsilon}}\in H^{1}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q))\cap L^{\infty}(0,\tau;H^{2}(Q)). Then, the compact embedding L4​(0,τ,H2​(Q))∩H1​(0,τ,L2​(Q))⊂L4​(0,τ,W1,4​(Q))L^{4}(0,\tau;H^{2}(Q))\cap H^{1}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q))\subset L^{4}(0,\tau;W^{1,4}(Q)), along with the Schauder Fixed point theorem and a priori estimates ensure the existence of a solution to the original nonlinear problem (1) for all ε>0{\varepsilon}>0. The regularity of the solutions ensures that uε,vε∈C⁡([0,τ],L2​(Q))u^{\varepsilon},\,v^{\varepsilon}\in C([0,\tau];L^{2}(Q)) for PP-a.s. ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega, and thus the initial conditions are satisfied.

We also remark that the a priori estimates are first derived for Galerkin approximations constructed by smooth eigenfunctions of the one-dimensional Laplace operator with Neumann boundary conditions. Then, using standard arguments pertaining to the weak convergence and lower semicontinuity of the norms involved, we also obtain the corresponding estimates for the solutions uεu^{\varepsilon} and vεv^{\varepsilon} of (1).

We remark that, provided Assumption 1, the solutions of (1) remain nonnegative for all times, see e.g. [41, 45]. To prove the required a priori estimates, we first consider ϕ=1\phi=1 and ψ=1\psi=1 as test functions in (3) and (4) to obtain

‖uε​(t)‖L1​(Q)=‖u0‖L1​(Q) for ​t≥0,\|u^{\varepsilon}(t)\|_{L^{1}(Q)}=\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(Q)}\qquad\text{ for }t\geq 0\;, (7)

and

Similarly, we show the uniqueness of the weak solution of (1) by considering the equations for the difference of two solutions and showing that they are equal a.e. in QτQ_{\tau} and PP-a.s. in Ω\Omega. ∎

4 Stochastic homogenization

In this section, we derive our main homogenization result for problem (1). The system of macroscopic equations is obtained in Theorem 15 by using the concept of stochastic two-scale convergence introduced in [52]. For the reader’s convenience we state the general definition of two-scale convergence by means of Palm measures, and then apply it to the specific context of the problem studied in this paper. In the following, we also make use of the notions of invariance and ergodicity, which we now define.

Definition 5.

A measurable function ff on Ω\Omega is said to be invariant for a dynamical system 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) if for each x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, f⁡(ω)=f⁡(𝒯⁡(x)​ω)f(\omega)=f({\mathcal{T}}(x)\omega), PP-a.s. on Ω\Omega.

Definition 6.

A dynamical system 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) is said to be ergodic, if every measurable function which is invariant for 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) is PP-a.s. equal to a constant.

The random environment described by the coefficients in (1) can also be characterized in terms of a random measure, which is defined as follows.

Definition 7.

Let (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}) be a measurable space and ℬ⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be the σ\sigma-algebra of Borel sets in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. A mapping μ~:Ω×ℬ⁡(ℝd)→ℝ+∪{∞}\tilde{\mu}:\Omega\times\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}\cup\{\infty\} is called a random measure on (ℝd,ℬ⁡(ℝd))(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d})) if the function μω​(A)=μ~​(ω,A)\mu_{\omega}(A)=\tilde{\mu}(\omega,A) is ℱ\mathcal{F}-measurable in ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega for each A∈ℬ⁡(ℝd)A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and a measure in A∈ℬ⁡(ℝd)A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) for each ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega.

Even though more general definitions of a random measure exist in the literature (see, e.g., [14] or [28]), in the remainder of the paper μω\mu_{\omega} will always denote a random measure on (ℝd,ℬ⁡(ℝd))(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d})).

Definition 8.

The Palm measure of the random measure μω\mu_{\omega} is the measure 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu} on (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}) defined by the relation

𝝁(A)=∫Ω∫ℝd𝕀[0,1)d(x)𝕀A(𝒯(x)ω)dμω(x)dP(ω),\boldsymbol{\mu}(A)=\int_{\Omega}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbb{I}_{[0,1)^{d}}(x)\,\mathbb{I}_{A}({\mathcal{T}}(x)\omega)\,d\mu_{\omega}(x)dP(\omega)\;, (28)

where 𝕀K\mathbb{I}_{K} denotes the characteristic function of the set KK.

The value of the notion of a Palm measure is that it allows for a generalization of Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem for stationary random measures. Specifically, given a dynamical system 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x), we say that the random measure μω\mu_{\omega} is stationary if for every ϕ∈C0∞​(ℝd)\phi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})

∫ℝdϕ⁡(y−x)​d​μω​(y)=∫ℝdϕ⁡(y)​d​μ𝒯⁡(x)​ω​(y).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\phi(y-x)\,d\mu_{\omega}(y)\,=\,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\phi(y)\,d\mu_{{\mathcal{T}}(x)\omega}(y)\;.

The intensity m⁡(μω)m(\mu_{\omega}) of a random measure μω\mu_{\omega} is defined by

m(μω)=∫Ω∫[0,1)ddμω(x)dP(ω).m(\mu_{\omega})=\int_{\Omega}\int_{[0,1)^{d}}\,d\mu_{\omega}(x)\,dP(\omega)\;. (29)
Theorem 9 (Ergodic theorem [52]).

Let the dynamical system 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) be ergodic and assume that the stationary random measure μω\mu_{\omega} has finite intensity m⁡(μω)>0m(\mu_{\omega})>0. Then

limt→∞1t​|A|​∫t​Ag⁡(𝒯⁡(x)​ω)​d​μω​(x)=∫Ωg⁡(ω)​𝑑𝝁​(ω) a.s. with respect to ​P\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t\,|A|}\int_{tA}g({\mathcal{T}}(x)\omega)d\mu_{\omega}(x)=\int_{\Omega}g(\omega)d\boldsymbol{\mu}(\omega)\quad\text{ a.s. with respect to }P (30)

for all bounded Borel sets AA, with volume |A|>0|A|>0, and all g∈L1​(Ω,𝛍)g\in L^{1}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}).

We remark that for 𝝁=P\boldsymbol{\mu}=P (i.e., d​μω​(x)=d​xd\mu_{\omega}(x)=dx), Theorem 9 reduces to the classical ergodic theorem of Birkhoff.

We now define the notion of stochastic two-scale convergence, which is one of the main tools used in proving Theorem 15. We consider the family of random measures

d​μωε​(x)=εd​d​μω​(xε).d\mu_{\omega}^{\varepsilon}(x)={\varepsilon}^{d}d\mu_{\omega}\left(\frac{x}{{\varepsilon}}\right)\;.

We remark that an immediate consequence of Theorem 9 is that on every compact subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, the family d​μωε​(x)d\mu^{\varepsilon}_{\omega}(x) converges weakly to the deterministic measure m⁡(μω)​d​xm(\mu_{\omega})\,dx a.s. with respect to PP as ε→0{\varepsilon}\to 0 (see, e.g., [52]).

Definition 10 (Stochastic two-scale convergence [21, 52]).

Let QQ be a domain in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) be an ergodic dynamical system, and 𝒯⁡(x)​ω~{\mathcal{T}}(x)\tilde{\omega} be a “typical trajectory,” i.e. one that satisfies equation (30) for all g∈C⁡(Ω)g\in C(\Omega). Then, we say that a sequence {vε}⊂L2​(0,τ,L2​(Q,μω~ε))\{v^{\varepsilon}\}\subset L^{2}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q,\mu_{\tilde{\omega}}^{\varepsilon})) converges stochastically two-scale to v∈L2​(0,τ,L2​(Q×Ω,d​x×d​𝝁​(ω)))v\in L^{2}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q\times\Omega,dx\times d\boldsymbol{\mu}(\omega))) if

lim supε→0∫0τ∫Q|vε​(t,x)|2​d​μω~ε​(x)​𝑑t<∞\limsup\limits_{{\varepsilon}\to 0}\int_{0}^{\tau}\int_{Q}|v^{\varepsilon}(t,x)|^{2}\,d\mu_{\tilde{\omega}}^{\varepsilon}(x)\,dt<\infty (31)

and

limε→0∫0τ∫Qvε​(t,x)​φ​(t,x)​b​(𝒯⁡(x/ε)​ω~)​d​μω~ε​(x)​𝑑t\displaystyle\lim\limits_{{\varepsilon}\to 0}\int_{0}^{\tau}\int_{Q}v^{\varepsilon}(t,x)\varphi(t,x)b({\mathcal{T}}(x/{\varepsilon})\tilde{\omega})\,d\mu^{\varepsilon}_{\tilde{\omega}}(x)dt (32)
=∫0τ∫Q∫Ωv⁡(t,x,ω)​φ​(t,x)​b​(ω)​𝑑𝝁​(ω)​𝑑x​𝑑t\displaystyle\hskip 113.81102pt=\int_{0}^{\tau}\int_{Q}\int_{\Omega}v(t,x,\omega)\varphi(t,x)b(\omega)\,d\boldsymbol{\mu}(\omega)dxdt

for all φ∈C0∞​([0,τ)×Q)\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{0}([0,\tau)\times Q) and b∈L2​(Ω,𝝁)b\in L^{2}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}).

It is evident that if Q⊂ℝdQ\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is bounded, each φ∈C∞​(Q¯τ)\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\overline{Q}_{\tau}) can be used as a test function in Definition 10. The concept of a “typical trajectory” in Definition 10 extends to realizations ω~∈Ω\tilde{\omega}\in\Omega. Specifically, we say that ω~∈Ω\tilde{\omega}\in\Omega is a “typical realization” if (30) holds true at ω~\tilde{\omega} for all g∈C⁡(Ω)g\in C(\Omega).

Theorem 11.

[21, 52] Every sequence {vε}⊂L2​(0,τ,L2​(Q,μω~ε))\{v^{\varepsilon}\}\subset L^{2}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q,\mu_{\tilde{\omega}}^{\varepsilon})) that satisfies (31) converges along a subsequence to some v∈L2​(0,τ,L2​(Q×Ω,d​x×d​𝛍​(ω)))v\in L^{2}(0,\tau;L^{2}(Q\times\Omega,dx\times d\boldsymbol{\mu}(\omega))) in the sense of stochastic two-scale convergence.

Before we proceed, we need to define a concept of stochastic derivative and the space H1​(Ω,𝝁)H^{1}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) for the Palm measure 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu}. First, we say that a function u∈C⁡(Ω)u\in C(\Omega) belongs to C1​(Ω)C^{1}(\Omega) if the limit

∂ωju⁡(ω)=limh→0u⁡(𝒯⁡(h​ej)​ω)−u⁡(ω)h\partial^{j}_{\omega}u(\omega)\,=\,\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{u({\mathcal{T}}(he_{j})\omega)-u(\omega)}{h}

exists and ∂ωju⁡(ω)∈C⁡(Ω)\partial^{j}_{\omega}u(\omega)\in C(\Omega). Then, the Sobolev space H1​(Ω,𝝁)H^{1}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) is defined as follows.

Definition 12.

[52] We say that a function u∈L2​(Ω,𝝁)u\in L^{2}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) belongs to H1​(Ω,𝝁)H^{1}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) and ∂ωu\partial_{\omega}u is a (stochastic) derivative of uu if there exists a sequence uk∈C1​(Ω)u_{k}\in C^{1}(\Omega) such that uk→uu_{k}\rightarrow u in L2​(Ω,𝝁)L^{2}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) and ∂ωjuk→∂ωju\partial^{j}_{\omega}u_{k}\rightarrow\partial^{j}_{\omega}u in L2​(Ω,𝝁)L^{2}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}).

In general, the stochastic derivative ∂ωu\partial_{\omega}u does not have to be unique (see [52] for counterexamples). We remark, however, that the particular setting of our problem yields the uniqueness of ∂ωu\partial_{\omega}u. We also define Lpot2​(Ω,𝝁)L^{2}_{\text{pot}}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) and Lsol2​(Ω,𝝁)L^{2}_{\text{sol}}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) to be the spaces of potential functions and divergence-free functions, respectively. More precisely,

Lpot2(Ω,𝝁)={∂ωu:u∈C1​(Ω)}¯ and Lsol2(Ω,𝝁)=(Lpot2(Ω,𝝁))⟂,L^{2}_{\text{pot}}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu})=\overline{\{\partial_{\omega}u\,:\,u\in C^{1}(\Omega)\}}\,\mbox{ and }\,L^{2}_{\text{sol}}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu})=\big(L^{2}_{\text{pot}}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu})\big)^{\perp},

where the closure in the definition of Lpot2​(Ω,𝝁)L^{2}_{\text{pot}}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) is with respect to the L2​(Ω,𝝁)L^{2}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) norm.

We now state two compactness results for the notion of stochastic two-scale convergence to be used in the following. Theorems 13 and 14 were proved in [52] in the more general setting of an arbitrary random measure. Here, the theorems are stated in the context of our problem, i.e. for a non-degenerate random measure μω\mu_{\omega} (see [52] for the definition of non-degeneracy).

Remark. For a non-degenerate measure, ∂ωj\partial_{\omega}^{j} denotes the generator of a strongly continuous group of unitary operators in L2​(Ω,𝝁)L^{2}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}) associated with 𝒯⁡(x){\mathcal{T}}(x) along the eje_{j} direction. The domains of ∂ωj\partial_{\omega}^{j}, with j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d, are dense in L2​(Ω,𝝁)L^{2}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu}). We let ∇ωu=(∂ω1u,…,∂ωdu)T\nabla_{\omega}u=(\partial_{\omega}^{1}u,\ldots,\partial_{\omega}^{d}u)^{T} and H1​(Ω,𝝁)={v∈L2​(Ω,𝝁):∇ωv∈L2​(Ω,𝝁)}H^{1}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu})=\{v\in L^{2}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu})\,:\,\nabla_{\omega}v\in L^{2}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu})\}.

Theorem 13.

[52] Let QQ be a domain in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and assume that μω\mu_{\omega} is a non-degenerate random measure and that the sequence {vε}⊂H1​(Q,μω~ε)\{v^{\varepsilon}\}\subset H^{1}(Q,\mu_{\tilde{\omega}}^{\varepsilon}) is such that

‖vε‖L2​(Q,μω~ε)≤C⁡(ω~),‖∇vε‖L2​(Q,μω~ε)≤C⁡(ω~).\|v^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(Q,\mu_{\tilde{\omega}}^{\varepsilon})}\leq C(\tilde{\omega})\;,\qquad\|\nabla v^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(Q,\mu_{\tilde{\omega}}^{\varepsilon})}\leq C(\tilde{\omega})\;.

Then there exist functions v∈H1​(Q)v\in H^{1}(Q) and v1∈L2​(Q,Lpot2​(Ω,𝛍))v_{1}\in L^{2}(Q;L^{2}_{\text{pot}}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu})) such that, up to a subsequence, the following hold:

vε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon} ⇀v\displaystyle\rightharpoonup v\,\quad stochastically two-scale,\displaystyle\text{ stochastically two-scale}, (33)
∇vε\displaystyle\nabla v^{\varepsilon} ⇀∇xv+v1\displaystyle\rightharpoonup\nabla_{x}v+v_{1}\qquad stochastically two-scale.\displaystyle\text{ stochastically two-scale}.
Theorem 14.

[52] Let QQ be a domain in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and assume that μω\mu_{\omega} is a non-degenerate random measure and that the sequence {vε}⊂H1​(Q,μω~ε)\{v^{\varepsilon}\}\subset H^{1}(Q,\mu_{\tilde{\omega}}^{\varepsilon}) is such that

Then there exists a function v∈L2​(Q,H1​(Ω,𝛍))v\in L^{2}(Q;H^{1}(\Omega,\boldsymbol{\mu})) such that, up to a subsequence, the following hold:

ε∇vε\displaystyle{\varepsilon}\nabla v^{\varepsilon} ⇀∇ωv\displaystyle\rightharpoonup\nabla_{\omega}v\qquad stochastically two-scale.\displaystyle\text{ stochastically two-scale}.

Similar results hold for {vε}⊂L2​(0,τ,H1​(Q,μω~ε))\{v^{\varepsilon}\}\subset L^{2}(0,\tau;H^{1}(Q,\mu_{\tilde{\omega}}^{\varepsilon})), where the time variable is considered as a parameter [21].

5 Periodic approximation of the effective coefficients

We now turn our attention to the problem of approximating the homogenized coefficients shown in (36) by means of a periodization procedure. The significance of such approximations is discussed in [5] and [42]. Here, we build upon the methods developed in [5] and consider the following periodization procedure.

We let Sρ=[0,ρ]dS_{\rho}=[0,\rho]^{d} for some ρ>0\rho>0, and for each ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega we consider the periodic functions

Then for PP-a.s. ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega, we consider the equations

u¯tε\displaystyle\bar{u}^{\varepsilon}_{t} =∇⋅(Du,perρ(x/ε,ω)∇u¯ε−χρper(x/ε,ω)u¯ε∇v¯ε)\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot(D_{u,\text{per}}^{\rho}(x/{\varepsilon},\omega)\nabla\bar{u}^{\varepsilon}-\chi^{\rho}_{\text{per}}(x/{\varepsilon},\omega)\bar{u}^{\varepsilon}\,\nabla\bar{v}^{\varepsilon}) in ​Qτ,\displaystyle\text{ in }Q_{\tau},
v¯tε\displaystyle\bar{v}^{\varepsilon}_{t} =∇⋅(Dv(x)∇v¯ε)−γv¯ε+αu¯ε\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot(D_{v}(x)\nabla\bar{v}^{\varepsilon})-\gamma\bar{v}^{\varepsilon}+\alpha\bar{u}^{\varepsilon} in ​Qτ,\displaystyle\text{ in }Q_{\tau},
∇u¯ε⋅n=0,∇v¯ε⋅n=0\displaystyle\nabla\bar{u}^{\varepsilon}\cdot n=0,\quad\nabla\bar{v}^{\varepsilon}\cdot n=0 on ​(0,τ)×∂Q.\displaystyle\text{ on }(0,\tau)\times\partial Q.

The equation for u¯ε\bar{u}^{\varepsilon} has periodic coefficients, and hence we can employ methods pertaining to periodic homogenization to obtain the effective coefficients for the corresponding macroscopic problem. However, since Du,perρ​(z,ω)D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(z,\omega) and χperρ​(z,ω)\chi^{\rho}_{\text{per}}(z,\omega) are not ergodic anymore, the effective coefficients are not deterministic (i.e., they depend on ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega).

The unit cell problems that are obtained from the periodic homogenization approach are: Find η¯jρ,η^jρ∈Hper1​(Sρ)\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{j},\,\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{j}\in H^{1}_{\text{per}}(S_{\rho}), for j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d, such that

∇z⋅(Du,perρ​(z,ω)​(∇zη¯jρ+ej))=0 in Sρ,∇z⋅(Du,perρ​(z,ω)​∇zη^jρ−χperρ​(z,ω)​ej)=0 in Sρ.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \nabla_{z}\cdot(D_{u,\text{per}}^{\rho}(z,\omega)(\nabla_{z}\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{j}+e_{j}))&=0\quad\text{ in }S_{\rho}\;,\\ \nabla_{z}\cdot(D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(z,\omega)\nabla_{z}\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{j}-\chi_{\text{per}}^{\rho}(z,\omega)e_{j})&=0\quad\text{ in }S_{\rho}\;.\end{aligned} (42)

Given the corrector functions η¯ρ,η^ρ∈Hper1​(Sρ)\bar{\eta}^{\rho},\,\,\hat{\eta}^{\rho}\in H^{1}_{\text{per}}(S_{\rho}), the effective coefficients are then defined by

Dω,i​jρ\displaystyle D^{\rho}_{\omega,ij} =\displaystyle= 1ρd​∫Sρ((Du,perρ​(z,ω)​∇zη¯iρ)j+Du,perρ​(z,ω)​δi​j)​𝑑z,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\rho^{d}}\int_{S_{\rho}}\big((D_{u,\text{per}}^{\rho}(z,\omega)\nabla_{z}\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{i})_{j}+D_{u,\text{per}}^{\rho}(z,\omega)\delta_{ij}\big)\,dz\;, (43)
χω,i​jρ\displaystyle\chi^{\rho}_{\omega,ij} =\displaystyle= −1ρd∫Sρ((Du,perρ(z,ω)∇zη^iρ)j−χperρ(z,ω)δi​j)dz,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{\rho^{d}}\int_{S_{\rho}}\big((D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(z,\omega)\nabla_{z}\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{i})_{j}-\chi_{\text{per}}^{\rho}(z,\omega)\delta_{ij}\big)\,dz\;, (44)

for i,j=1,…,di,j=1,\ldots,d, and the macroscopic equations read

∂tuρ=∇⋅(Dρω∇uρ−χρωuρ∇vρ)\displaystyle\partial_{t}u^{\rho}=\nabla\cdot(D^{\rho}_{\omega}\,\nabla u^{\rho}-\chi^{\rho}_{\omega}\,u^{\rho}\,\nabla v^{\rho}) in ​Qτ,\displaystyle\text{ in }\,\,Q_{\tau},
∂tvρ=∇⋅(Dv(x)∇vρ)−γvρ+αuρ\displaystyle\partial_{t}v^{\rho}=\nabla\cdot(D_{v}(x)\nabla v^{\rho})-\gamma\,v^{\rho}+\alpha\,u^{\rho} in ​Qτ,\displaystyle\text{ in }\,\,Q_{\tau},
(Dρω∇uρ−χρωuρ∇vρ)⋅n=0,∇vρ⋅n=0\displaystyle(D^{\rho}_{\omega}\,\nabla u^{\rho}-\chi^{\rho}_{\omega}\,u^{\rho}\,\nabla v^{\rho})\cdot n=0,\qquad\nabla v^{\rho}\cdot n=0\quad on ​(0,τ)×∂Q\displaystyle\text{ on }\,\,(0,\tau)\times\partial Q

for PP-a.s. ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega.

The following theorem is the key result of this section. It guarantees the convergence of the effective coefficients obtained by periodic approximation to the original effective coefficients obtained from the stochastic homogenization in the previous section.

Theorem 16.

Let DωρD^{\rho}_{\omega} and χωρ\chi^{\rho}_{\omega} be the effective coefficients obtained in (43) and (44), respectively. Then for D∗D^{\ast} and χ∗\chi^{\ast} as in (36), the following hold true

limρ→∞Dω,i​jρ=Di​j∗P-a.s.,limρ→∞χω,i​jρ=χi​j∗P-a.s.,i,j=1,…,d.\lim\limits_{\rho\to\infty}D^{\rho}_{\omega,ij}=D^{\ast}_{ij}\quad\text{P-a.s.},\qquad\lim\limits_{\rho\to\infty}\chi^{\rho}_{\omega,ij}=\chi^{\ast}_{ij}\quad\text{P-a.s.},\quad i,j=1,\ldots,d. (45)
Proof.

First, we consider in S1=[0,1]S_{1}=[0,1] the auxiliary problems

{∇x⋅(Du,perρ​(ρ​x,ω)​(∇xw¯jρ+ej))=0 in ​S1,w¯jρS1−periodic,∫S1w¯jρ​(x)​dx=0,\displaystyle\begin{cases}\nabla_{x}\cdot\big(D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(\rho x,\omega)(\nabla_{x}\bar{w}^{\rho}_{j}+e_{j})\big)=0\hskip 48.36958pt\text{ in }\,S_{1}\;,\\ \bar{w}^{\rho}_{j}\qquad S_{1}-\text{periodic},\hskip 54.06006pt\int_{S_{1}}\bar{w}^{\rho}_{j}(x)\,dx=0\;,\end{cases} (46)
{∇x⋅(Du,perρ​(ρ​x,ω)​∇xw^jρ−χperρ​(ρ​x,ω)​ej)=0 in ​S1,w^jρS1−periodic,∫S1w^jρ​(x)​dx=0.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\nabla_{x}\cdot\big(D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(\rho x,\omega)\nabla_{x}\hat{w}^{\rho}_{j}-\chi^{\rho}_{\text{per}}(\rho x,\omega)e_{j}\big)=0\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ in }\,S_{1}\;,\\ \hat{w}^{\rho}_{j}\qquad S_{1}-\text{periodic},\hskip 54.06006pt\int_{S_{1}}\hat{w}^{\rho}_{j}(x)dx=0\;.\end{cases} (47)

From the definition of Du,perρD^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}} we have that Du,perρ​(ρ​x,ω)=Du​(ρ​x,ω)D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(\rho x,\omega)=D_{u}(\rho x,\omega) in S1S_{1}. Then, for ρ=1/ε\rho=1/{\varepsilon} and Q=S1Q=S_{1}, one can apply the stochastic homogenization results of Section 4 to problems (46) and (47) to obtain the effective macroscopic equations

∇x⋅(D∗​(∇xw¯j+ej))=0 in ​S1,w¯jS1−periodic,∫S1w¯j​(x)​dx=0,∇x⋅(D∗​∇xw^j−χ∗​ej)=0 in ​S1,w^jS1−periodic,∫S1w^j​(x)​dx=0,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \nabla_{x}\cdot(D^{\ast}(\nabla_{x}\bar{w}_{j}+e_{j}))=0\quad\text{ in }S_{1}\;,\quad\bar{w}_{j}\quad S_{1}-\text{periodic},\,\,\int_{S_{1}}\bar{w}_{j}(x)\,dx=0\;,\\ \nabla_{x}\cdot(D^{\ast}\nabla_{x}\hat{w}_{j}-\chi^{\ast}e_{j})=0\quad\text{ in }S_{1}\;,\quad\hat{w}_{j}\quad S_{1}-\text{periodic},\,\,\int_{S_{1}}\hat{w}_{j}(x)\,dx=0\;,\end{aligned} (48)

where j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d, and D∗D^{\ast} and χ∗\chi^{\ast} are given by (36).

We then consider the coordinate transformation y=z/ρy=z/\rho in equations (42), transforming SρS_{\rho} to the unit cube S1S_{1}. We let η¯0,jρ​(y)=1ρ​η¯jρ​(ρ​y)\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}(y)=\frac{1}{\rho}\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{j}(\rho y) and η^0,jρ​(y)=1ρ​η^jρ​(ρ​y)\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}(y)=\frac{1}{\rho}\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{j}(\rho y), and rewrite the equations in (42) as

∇y⋅(Du,perρ​(ρ​y,ω)​(∇yη¯0,jρ+ej))=0 in ​S1,\displaystyle\nabla_{y}\cdot(D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(\rho y,\omega)(\nabla_{y}\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}+e_{j}))=0\hskip 64.01869pt\text{ in }\,S_{1}, (49)
∇y⋅(Du,perρ​(ρ​y,ω)​∇yη^0,jρ−χperρ​(ρ​y,ω)​ej)=0 in ​S1,\displaystyle\nabla_{y}\cdot(D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(\rho y,\omega)\nabla_{y}\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}-\chi^{\rho}_{\text{per}}(\rho y,\omega)e_{j})=0\quad\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ in }\,S_{1}, (50)

where η¯0,jρ\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j} and η^0,jρ\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j} are S1S_{1}-periodic functions, j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d. The solutions of (49) and (50) are unique up to an additive constant, which we fix by considering ∫S1η¯0,jρ​(y)​𝑑y=0\int_{S_{1}}\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}(y)dy=0 and ∫S1η^0,jρ​(y)​𝑑y=0\int_{S_{1}}\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}(y)dy=0. Taking η¯0ρ\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{0} and η^0ρ\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0} as test functions in (49) and (50), respectively, using Assumption 1 on the coefficients D~u\widetilde{D}_{u} and χ~\widetilde{\chi}, and applying the Poincaré inequality we obtain the following a priori estimates uniformly in ρ\rho

∥η¯ρ0,j∥H1​(S1)≤C,∥η^ρ0,j∥H1​(S1)≤C,j=1,…,d.\|\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}\|_{H^{1}(S_{1})}\leq C\;,\quad\|\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}\|_{H^{1}(S_{1})}\leq C,\quad j=1,\ldots,d\;. (51)

Thus, we have that η¯0,jρ\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j} and η^0,jρ\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j} converge weakly in Hper1​(S1)H^{1}_{\text{per}}(S_{1}) to η¯j∞\bar{\eta}^{\infty}_{j} and η^j∞\hat{\eta}^{\infty}_{j}, respectively, as ρ→∞\rho\to\infty, with j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d. We also have that η¯0,jρ\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j} and η^0,jρ\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j} converge stochastically two-scale to the same limit functions η¯j∞=η¯j∞​(y)\bar{\eta}^{\infty}_{j}=\bar{\eta}^{\infty}_{j}(y) and η^j∞=η^j∞​(y)\hat{\eta}^{\infty}_{j}=\hat{\eta}^{\infty}_{j}(y), with j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d. Then, considering the results on the stochastic homogenization of equations (46) and (47), we obtain that η¯j∞\bar{\eta}^{\infty}_{j} and η^j∞\hat{\eta}^{\infty}_{j} satisfy

Du,perρ​(ρ​y,ω)​(∇yη¯0,jρ+ej)⇀D∗​(∇yη¯j∞+ej) weakly in ​L2​(S1),Du,perρ​(ρ​y,ω)​∇yη^0,jρ−χperρ​(ρ​y,ω)​ej⇀D∗​∇yη^j∞−χ∗​ej weakly in ​L2​(S1),\displaystyle\quad\begin{aligned} D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(\rho y,\omega)(\nabla_{y}\bar{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}+e_{j})&\rightharpoonup&D^{\ast}(\nabla_{y}\bar{\eta}^{\infty}_{j}+e_{j})&\,\,\text{ weakly in }\,L^{2}(S_{1}),\\ D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(\rho y,\omega)\nabla_{y}\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}-\chi^{\rho}_{\text{per}}(\rho y,\omega)e_{j}&\rightharpoonup&D^{\ast}\nabla_{y}\hat{\eta}^{\infty}_{j}-\chi^{\ast}e_{j}\,&\,\,\text{ weakly in }\,L^{2}(S_{1}),\end{aligned} (53)

as ρ→∞\rho\to\infty, for PP-a.s. ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega and j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d. Finally, since the only periodic solutions of (52) with zero average are η¯j∞​(y)=0\bar{\eta}^{\infty}_{j}(y)=0 and η^j∞​(y)=0\hat{\eta}^{\infty}_{j}(y)=0 for y∈S1y\in S_{1}, it follows from (53) that

χρω,j=−\displaystyle\chi^{\rho}_{\omega,j}=- ∫S1(Du,perρ​(ρ​y,ω)​∇yη^0,jρ−χperρ​(ρ​y,ω)​ej)​𝑑y\displaystyle\int_{S_{1}}\big(D^{\rho}_{u,\text{per}}(\rho y,\omega)\nabla_{y}\hat{\eta}^{\rho}_{0,j}-\chi^{\rho}_{\text{per}}(\rho y,\omega)e_{j}\big)\,dy →\displaystyle\to ∫S1χ∗​ej​dy=χj∗,\displaystyle\int_{S_{1}}\chi^{\ast}e_{j}dy=\chi^{\ast}_{j}\;,

as ρ→∞\rho\to\infty, for PP-a.s. ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega and j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d. This proves the convergence results stated in the theorem. ∎
